li.a: WikiMafia: Strage di Portella della Ginestra
Ethica Societas: 1 maggio 1947, la strage di Portella delle Ginestre
Sempre per la verita: Portella della Ginestra
Edscuola: Le stragi del 47 (police reports of 1947)
PalermoToday: the 75th anniversary ceremony at Portella della Ginestra

content.p: On 1 May 1947, around two thousand peasants and workers walked, rode and drove carts up to a high plain in western Sicily to celebrate the first Labour Day of the Italian republic. Within minutes of the first speech, gunfire from the slopes above began to cut into the crowd. Eleven people died and dozens were wounded. The courts that later judged the case put the blame on the band of the bandit Salvatore Giuliano and found no instigators behind it. Historians and politicians have disputed that conclusion, and the question of who ordered the attack still has no judicial answer nearly eighty years on.
content.h2: A holiday returns, and an election result
content.p: Under Fascism the workers' holiday had been folded into the celebration of the founding of Rome on 21 April, so 1 May 1947 was the first time in years that the old date could be marked openly. The Ethica Societas journal and the Sempre per la verita site both note that the place had its own history: decades earlier the Socialist organiser Nicola Barbato had spoken there, and the police report says the platform used in 1947 was the rock from which the propagandist Barbato had spoken in the years before Fascism.

The gathering was also a celebration of an election. On 20 April the Popular Bloc, the alliance of Communists and Socialists, had won the Sicilian regional vote, taking about 32 percent against about 20 percent for Christian Democracy, according to Sempre per la verita; Ethica Societas puts the Bloc at 29 of 90 seats against 21 for the Christian Democrats. The marchers were also calling for land reform. In October 1944 the Communist agriculture minister Fausto Gullo had legalised the occupation of uncultivated land and set a split of the harvest that favoured farm workers over owners. Both Ethica Societas and Sempre per la verita describe this as a perceived threat to the political balance in Sicily, a balance that, they say, the mafia also helped to manage.

The people who came were poor. Ethica Societas reports that some survivors later said they had joined in hope of getting something to eat. The police report written within days of the shooting notes that the groups from San Giuseppe Jato and San Cipirello arrived around nine, led by the mayor of San Cipirello, Pasquale Sciortino, and that they spread across the meadows to rest and eat while they waited. A cart carrying about 200 rations of bread, wine and artichokes for poorer comrades had been brought up and parked near the platform, according to one witness statement attached to the report.

According to Sempre per la verita and Ethica Societas, the scheduled speaker was the Communist deputy Girolamo Li Causi; the police report instead names an official speaker, Pedalino of the Federterra, as the one awaited. While the crowd waited, Giacomo Schirò, a shoemaker from San Giuseppe Jato and secretary of the local Socialist section, began to speak. The police report says he had said only a few sentences, and had drawn applause, when shooting began. Nobody understood at first. Many people thought they were hearing fireworks let off for the holiday.

The firing continued in bursts with short pauses. The report describes a young man from Piana degli Albanesi falling bleeding beside the mayor of San Cipirello, then other young people being hit, and animals grazing nearby going down as well. Only then did the crowd realise they were being shot at; people scattered, or tried to take cover behind the big stones. Ethica Societas says the youngest were hit hardest, because the older people threw themselves to the ground, and that the almost complete lack of cover left the families exposed. Sempre per la verita says the bursts of machine-gun fire came from Monte Pelavet and lasted about a quarter of an hour.

The death toll depends on the source. WikiMafia and Italia.it give 11 dead; WikiMafia adds 27 seriously wounded, while Sempre per la verita speaks of about thirty injured and Italia.it of more than 30. Ethica Societas writes that 11 died at once, more than 30 were seriously wounded, and six of those later died. The memorial's list, as reproduced by Sempre per la verita, gives seven who died on the spot (Francesco Vicari and Giovanni Megna among them, with Margherita Clesceri, Giorgio Cusenza, Castrense Intravaia, Vincenza La Fata and Serafino Lascari). It names four who died of their wounds a few days later: Vito Allotta, Giuseppe Di Maggio, Filippo Di Salvo and Giovanni Grifò. The same page lists further people who died afterwards, among them Provvidenza Greco, Vincenza Spina and Vincenzo La Rocca, and says Vita Dorangricchia died nine months later of wounds suffered that day. It also counts among the dead of 1 May Emanuele Busellini, a farm guard the bandits are said to have met on the road to the site and killed.

The statements gathered in the days after the shooting, preserved in the police reports published by Edscuola, are among the most direct evidence. A group of five young men and a woman had gone to a hidden spot more than a kilometre from the plain to eat. They told police that after the shooting they saw armed men coming down the Pizzuta slope in small groups, and that one of the last said, in Sicilian, something like a reproach asking the others what they had done. None of them said they recognised anyone. One of the young men rode a mule to find a carabiniere sergeant, who came back with him, but the gunmen had already gone.

A young farmer, Alberto Borruso, told police that he had gone up the slope to cut grass for his mule and took cover behind a heap of stones. He said he saw a man firing bursts from a submachine gun and recognised him as Benedetto Gricoli, known as Troia. Police arrested four men from San Giuseppe Jato on the strength of this and a second statement, and the report lists them as Giuseppe Troia, Salvatore Romano, Elia Marino and Pietro Benedetto Gricoli. Ethica Societas says that they were named as perpetrators by eyewitnesses, but were later released at the investigative stage. Another woman told police that, that morning, she had heard one of three men sitting outside a house say it would be a good morning to set up a machine gun and leave them all there.

The mayor of San Cipirello told police he could explain the attack only as a political reaction. He recalled that after the election a former carabinieri officer had warned him that celebrations should be avoided, and that a local mafia boss had said at a rally that a Bloc victory would mean blood. He also handed over an anonymous letter naming four men as the killers. The report records that two of them were already in custody.

In the first sweep Ethica Societas counts 175 people detained and then freed. At the end of June a turn seemed to come: hunters whom the bandits had held before the assault identified Giuliano, Salvatore Ferreri, known as Fra Diavolo, and the brothers Salvatore and Fedele Pianelli. Another man, Francesco Gaglio, was arrested after a confession from one of them naming him as a participant. According to Ethica Societas, all the other people arrested as accomplices were eventually cleared.
content.h2: The official line and its critics
content.p: According to WikiMafia, the first reaction was a general strike called by the CGIL union, which accused the big landowners of wanting to drown the workers' organisations in blood. The chief police inspector for Sicily, Ettore Messana, played the event down as a local episode. On 2 May the Christian Democrat interior minister, Mario Scelba, read Messana's telegram to the Constituent Assembly and named Giuliano and his band as the only culprits, WikiMafia says.

WikiMafia and Sempre per la verita both argue that the way the attack was carried out points beyond a bandit gang: encircling the crowd and using weapons of war amounted, they say, to a military action studied in detail that went beyond the capacity of Giuliano and his men. WikiMafia notes that the use of grenades was left out of the report by the carabinieri sergeants, and says that if all those weapons had been meant only for the crowd the toll would have been higher. These are the arguments of those sources, not findings of a court.

In the weeks after Portella, Ethica Societas reports, machine guns and grenades were used against Communist Party offices in Monreale, Carini, Cinisi, Terrasini, Borgetto, Partinico, San Giuseppe Jato and San Cipirello. Sempre per la verita says one person was killed and many wounded, and that leaflets signed by Giuliano called on people to rise against communism. Ethica Societas adds that Giuliano wrote to US President Truman offering to fight Bolshevism and asking for Sicily to be annexed to the United States.
content.h2: Trials, a death in a courtyard, and a poisoning
content.p: Ethica Societas says Giuliano first denied involvement, then admitted it in an interview with the journalist Jacopo Rizza and in two memoranda sent to magistrates in 1950. In the first, it says, he took responsibility and claimed the victims were the result of his men's mistaken aim; in the second he cleared Scelba of the charge of having ordered the attack. Letters exchanged between the bandit and Li Causi, made public, contained veiled accusations against Scelba. In 1948 Giuliano had also written to the newspaper L'Unita, hinting at his relations with prominent politicians, according to WikiMafia.

On 5 July 1950, Giuliano was found dead in the courtyard of a lawyer's house in Castelvetrano. An Interior Ministry statement said he had been killed in a night shoot-out with carabinieri under Captain Antonino Perenze. The journalist Tommaso Besozzi challenged that account in the weekly L'Europeo under a title saying that the only certainty was that he was dead, pointing to gaps in the carabinieri version and naming Giuliano's lieutenant Gaspare Pisciotta as the killer, WikiMafia reports.

The trial began in Palermo in 1950 and was moved to Viterbo, Ethica Societas says, on grounds of legitimate suspicion; it describes it as one of the first trials to grip the national press. At Viterbo, WikiMafia says, Pisciotta claimed to have killed Giuliano himself, and named the deputies Bernardo Mattarella, Gianfranco Alliata, Tommaso Leone Marchesano and Scelba as political instigators. In the words WikiMafia quotes, he said that bandits, mafiosi and carabinieri had all been the same thing. On 9 February 1954 Pisciotta was poisoned with a strychnine-laced coffee in the Ucciardone prison, before he could testify about Portella to the prosecutor Pietro Scaglione.

The sources disagree over the date of the Viterbo verdict: WikiMafia and Sempre per la verita say 1952, while Ethica Societas says 1955. WikiMafia and Sempre per la verita say the judgments at Viterbo and Rome (1956) held only Giuliano and his men responsible, ignored testimony pointing to other accomplices, including that of four hunters from the Giuliano band caught on the Pelavet rocks the same day, and denied that there were instigators. Ethica Societas likewise says the sentence held Giuliano's group responsible, and the Edscuola page describes the final judgments as declaring that no instigators existed.

The site is now a place of remembrance. A memorial stands on the plain, and Italia.it calls Portella della Ginestra a symbol of resistance to the mafia and of commitment to social justice. In 2022, for the 75th anniversary, thousands took part in a march organised by the CGIL, laying a wreath at the victims' chapel in the Piana degli Albanesi cemetery before processing to the Barbato rock, where the 90-year-old survivor Serafino Petta read out the names of the dead. The union said again that it was demanding truth and justice about what it called the first state massacre of the Italian republic. Palermo's mayor Leoluca Orlando called it the first example of the strategy of tension in Italy, and said that a historical and legal truth was still missing. Ethica Societas concludes that, despite the verdicts, it is still not certain who the real instigators were.
